Triangles over a base

The definition of functors over a base remembers the identification making the triangle commute. This note explains how that identification is retained when passing to the relative mapping anima. Assume the Chapter 1 structures, including mapping animae, functor categories and pullbacks. All categories and functors below are absolute.

Fix \(f\colon C\to S\) and \(g\colon D\to S\). Write a functor over \(S\) as \(u=(h,\theta )\), where \(h\colon C\to D\) and \(\theta \colon gh=f\). We orient the triangle towards \(f\), as in the code; inverting \(\theta \) gives the convention in the book. For \(v=(k,\psi )\), a comparison \(u\simeq _S v\) consists of \(\alpha \colon h=k\) and a specified identification \[ \psi \cdot (g\alpha )=\theta . \] Here \(g\alpha \) denotes postcomposition of the identification by \(g\), and \(\beta \cdot \alpha \) means first \(\alpha \), then \(\beta \).

Supplementary Lemma 1. A triangle \(u\) has a name \(\ulcorner u\urcorner \) in \(\Map _S(C,D)\). A point \(x\) of this anima determines a triangle \(\operatorname {decode}(x)\). There are comparisons \[ \ulcorner \operatorname {decode}(x)\urcorner =x, \qquad \operatorname {decode}(\ulcorner u\urcorner )\simeq _S u. \]

Proof idea

The category \(\Fun _S(C,D)\) is the pullback of \(g_*\colon \Fun (C,D)\to \Fun (C,S)\) along the point naming \(f\). Name \(h\) in the first factor and use the identity of the terminal category in the second. Naming \(\theta \), followed by the postcomposition and unit comparisons, supplies the matching of this cone. The map converting \(\theta \) into that matching is an equivalence of identification animae.

Conversely, decode the first leg of a point of the pullback, normalize its terminal leg, and lift its matching through this equivalence. The pullback computation and reconstruction comparisons give the two displayed formulas. For the second formula, the matching comparison also recovers the specified triangle. Passing to the core gives the statement for \(\Map _S(C,D)\). □

Supplementary Lemma 2. A comparison \(u\simeq _S v\) gives an identification \(\ulcorner u\urcorner =\ulcorner v\urcorner \). Conversely, an identification of these names gives a comparison \(u\simeq _S v\).

Proof idea

Name the underlying identification \(\alpha \). Its equation over \(S\) becomes the matching equation for a comparison of the two named pullback cones. Lift that whole cone comparison and then name the result in the core.

In the reverse direction, extract a cone comparison from the identification of names. Its terminal component is identified with the identity. Lift the other component through the naming equivalence. Reflecting the matching equation through the equivalence used in Supplementary Lemma 1 gives exactly \(\psi \cdot (g\alpha )=\theta \). These constructions provide comparisons in both directions; the linked results here do not identify the two operations on comparison data as mutual inverses with their specified higher witnesses. □

Supplementary Lemma 3. Compose functors over \(S\) by pasting their triangles, with the associator inserted at the composite. The ordinary associator and the left and right unit identifications then give comparisons over \(S\).

Proof idea

For \(u=(h,\theta )\colon f\to g\) and \(v=(k,\psi )\colon g\to l\), the composite triangle follows the route \[ l(kh)\simeq (lk)h\xrightarrow {\psi h}gh\xrightarrow {\theta }f. \] For three functors, the two pasted routes are compared by the projection-square pentagon calculation. The unit cases use the corresponding triangle and unit calculations. These prove compatibility of the displayed associator and unit identifications with the triangles over \(S\). A pentagon among these relative associators is a further assertion, not part of this lemma. □
